_meta.note: Which of index3's translations a speaker still has to look at, and at what exactly. Every language with an `atlas` block in i18n.json appears here; tests/test_i18n_atlas.mjs fails on one that does not.
_meta.why: The prose was written against what could be sourced. Where a term for a computing concept could not be sourced, a transparent compound was coined from the language's own roots — which is legitimate in an agglutinative language and is also exactly the kind of thing that reads as fluent to someone who does not speak it and as nonsense to someone who does. Counting the coinages is the difference between a draft a speaker can review in an afternoon and one they would have to re-read line by line.
_meta.coined: term → the concept it was made for. They are also listed in the header comment of the language's own examples/graphics/mandelbrot/<id>.zy, which the page does not display.
_meta.not_a_score: A short list does not mean the prose is right, only that its nouns are attested. Nothing here has been read by a speaker.
_meta.attested: The terms taken from the language as it is written, not made here. `coined` against `attested` is the ratio that matters: where coinages outnumber attested terms, what is on the page is a draft with the shape of the language and mostly invented nouns, and a speaker is not reviewing it — they are writing it.
_meta.tags: Where an entry's BCP-47 code stands in for a language the site names generically, it says so in the note. An approximate tag still names the right language; the raw id is not a language tag at all.

english.note: The base. Everything else is measured against it.

spanish.note: Written by the project. `castellano` reads this block by alias.

portugues_eu.note: pt-PT. Differs from pt-BR on everyday computing words: `limpar o ecrã` vs `limpar a tela`.

french.note: `échappement` is the standard French term for the Mandelbrot escape-time algorithm, not a coinage.

haitian_creole.note: Official IPN orthography. Technical terms follow the French lexifier, which is what Kreyòl does.

jamaican_patois.note: No coinages: this is respelling, not coining. The concept names a Patwa speaker uses are the English ones, and `if` genuinely is `if`. What changed is the orthography, which is the language's own.

wayuu.note: Twelve coined against four attested — the ratio is inverted here, and that changes what this is. `ayaawase`/`ayaawaa` are derived from the attested `ayaawataa` (to measure, to mark); the rest are built from roots without a computing sense in any source I could reach. BCP-47 `guc`, which is Wayuu exactly.

embera.note: Thirteen coined against six attested. Emberá has among the thinnest published computing register of any language on this list; the prose here has the grammar and mostly invented nouns. BCP-47 `emp` is Northern Emberá standing in for an entry the site names only `Embera`.

yanomami.note: Fourteen coined against six attested — the furthest from a translation of anything on this list. Yanomami is several varieties with no shared written standard; BCP-47 `wca` is the Brazilian one standing in for all of them. This is a draft that needs writing, not reviewing.

tigrinya.note: Every term is the ordinary Tigrinya one. ረድፍታት rows, ዓምድታት columns, መስትያት mirror, ስጉምቲ step, መፍትሕ key, ምህዳም to flee. The terminal dimensions use ቁመት/ወርዲ and the plane ንውሓት/ስፍሓት, four distinct everyday words. Nothing was coined.

luganda.note: Every term is the ordinary Luganda one. ennyiriri rows, empagi columns (a pillar), endabirwamu mirror, omutendera step, ekisumuluzo key, dduka to run. The ramp is named obubonero (signs) so the single glyph can stay akabonero. Nothing was coined.

setswana.note: Almost every term is the ordinary Setswana one: mela rows, seipone mirror, kgato step, senotlolo key, tshaba to flee, and matshwao/letshwao for the ramp and the single glyph. ONE IS A LOAN: dikholomo, a naturalised borrowing of English 'column'. It is in ordinary use in Setswana tables and it is not a coinage, but a speaker should confirm it: no non-loan Setswana term for a table column was found.

coined.samp: column — coined here from samp 'to plant, to erect (a post)'. No attested Wolof term for a table column was found; a speaker should replace this if one exists.

wolof.note: Most terms are ordinary Wolof: rëdd rows, seetu mirror, digg middle, daw to flee, caabi key (a fully naturalised borrowing). TWO THINGS A SPEAKER SHOULD CHECK. First, màndargaYi and meloYi are the noun plus the plural article yi ('màndarga yi', 'melo yi') written closed up, because an identifier cannot hold a space — the words are ordinary, the spelling is an accommodation. Second, pas is the everyday French borrowing for a step. ONE COINAGE: samp, for column.

coined.jɔyɔrɔw: columns — coined here from jɔ 'to stand' + yɔrɔ 'place'. No attested Bambara term for a table column was found; a speaker should replace this if one exists.

bambara.note: The core is ordinary Bambara: taamasiɲɛnw/taamasiɲɛn for the ramp and the glyph, boli to run, cɛmancɛ middle, sen step, konnɛgɛ key (door-iron), janya and bonya for length and size. THREE ARE FRENCH BORROWINGS in everyday use, not coinages: kulɛri colour, layini line, gilasi mirror. ONE COINAGE: jɔyɔrɔw, for columns.

coined.tuggorɗe: columns — coined here as the plural of tuggordu, a prop or support. No attested Fulfulde term for a table column was found.
coined.tappol: step — coined here from tappude 'to tread'. The derivation is regular but the noun itself was not confirmed in a source; a speaker should check it.

fula.note: Most terms are ordinary Fulfulde: diide rows, daarorgal mirror, hakkunde middle, coktirgal key, dogde to run, juutol and yaajol for length and width, and maandeeji/maande for the ramp and the glyph. ONE SEMANTIC EXTENSION: noone, which means kind or sort and is used here for colour. TWO COINAGES: tuggorɗe and tappol.

nigerian_pidgin.note: Nothing was coined, and nothing was left untranslated either. Naijá is an English-lexified creole, so ladda, layn, kolom, mak, kala, step and ki look like English words because they ARE the Naijá words, written in Naijá orthography — the same argument as Jamaican Patois. What is NOT Naijá is the front-page claim 'No keyword.', which this page's hero corrects to 'No wɔd. / Na sain alone.' The sweep still reports 14 of 16 concept names as English for this entry; that is a fact about the entry's ops table, not about this program.

arabic.note: Every term is the ordinary Arabic one. صفوف rows, أعمدة columns, مرآة mirror, خطوة step, مفتاح key, هروب escape. The terminal dimensions use علو/عرض and the plane ارتفاع/اتساع, four distinct everyday words. Nothing was coined. This is the first right-to-left sample program: the identifiers are RTL, the marks are not, and the page pins every code pane to direction:ltr so the file is shown in its own order.

hebrew.note: Every term is the ordinary Hebrew one. שורות rows, עמודות columns, מראה mirror, צעד step, מקש key, בריחה escape. The two plane spans are compounds of ordinary words joined with an underscore, since an identifier cannot hold a space. Nothing was coined.

persian.note: Every term is the ordinary Persian one. سطرها rows, ستون‌ها columns, آینه mirror, گام step, کلید key, گریز escape. Two identifiers carry U+200C, the zero-width non-joiner Persian spells with — رنگ‌ها and ستون‌ها — which is why the joiners had to be admitted into the identifier rule. Nothing was coined.

Several strings match the English word for word (condition, collection, meta) because Interlingua's vocabulary is the international one — that is the language working, not a gap.

lojban.note: The core is attested gismu: salpo slope, skari colour, cliva to leave, minra mirror, midju middle, stapa step, batke key, sinxa sign, clani long, ganra wide. FIVE THINGS A SPEAKER SHOULD CHECK, none of them invented words. roskari is `ro skari` (all colours) written closed up, because an identifier cannot hold a space, so the single tint can stay skari. pinta (horizontal) and sraji (vertical) are used as the counts of rows and columns — a semantic extension of two gismu, not a new one. ganra_pixra and clani_pixra join two gismu with an underscore for the same spacing reason.

toki_pona.note: toki pona has about 120 words and no geometry vocabulary, so almost every name here is a compound of ordinary words written closed up — the language's normal way of saying a new thing, and an identifier cannot hold the space. sitelenMute many-symbols, kuleMute many-colours, pokaLipu side-of-the-sheet, suliLipu height-of-the-sheet, supaLukin looking-surface for the mirror, palisa a long rigid thing for a column, noka a foot used for a step. Nothing was invented; every part is in the word list. A speaker should still check that each compound reads the way it is meant to.

emoji.note: The identifiers are emoji, and both engines take them: 🪜 the ramp, 🌈 the colours, 🏃 escape, ➡ rows, ⬇ columns, 🪞 the mirror, 👣 the step, 🔑 the key. That is the site's existing convention for this entry — emoji leading, English behind — carried into a program that runs. Nothing was coined. Verified against the lexer first: a bare emoji, two emoji in a row, a letter plus an emoji and an underscore plus an emoji all parse and run.

coined.leghwI: mirror — coined here from legh (to see) plus the agentive -wI', so 'seer'. Klingon has no canonical noun for a mirror.

klingon.note: Most terms are canonical Klingon: Degh insignia/symbol, rItlh pigment, nargh to escape, tlhegh line, naQ staff (used for a column), botlh middle, chuq range, ngaQHa'moHwI' the unlocker for a key. FIVE ARE CANONICAL WORDS PUT TO A NEW USE: 'ab (be tall) and Dop (side) as the terminal's height and width, the two underscore compounds built on chuq, and qam (foot) for a step. ONE COINAGE: leghwI', for the mirror.

coined.: mirror — the same coinage as the Latin-script Klingon entry (leghwI'), transliterated.

klingon_piqad.note: Not written but GENERATED: every string is the Klingon entry transliterated into the CSUR pIqaD block (U+F8D0–U+F8E9), longest-match first so tlh, ch, gh and ng are single characters. HTML markup and the contents of <code> and <i> are left alone, because those hold the other languages' keywords and must stay Latin. The transliteration is checked by decoding it back: it returns the Latin entry exactly. The same script produced the sample program, which decodes back to klingon.zy character for character.
